problemText: Which of the following is the correct definition of the geosphere?
choices: All of Earth's solid and rocky material, including the crust, mantle, core, mountains, soil, and ocean floor
The layer of gases surrounding Earth that is composed mainly of nitrogen and oxygen and extends high above the land and ocean
All of Earth's water in its various forms, including water found in oceans, lakes, rivers, ice sheets, and groundwater beneath the surface
Every living organism on Earth and all the different environments and habitats in which those living things exist and interact
hints: The word 'geo' refers to Earth and rock.
Look for the choice that describes solid material.

problemText: A student observes snow melting on a mountainside during spring and flowing downhill as water into a valley stream. Which two spheres are interacting in this process?
choices: The atmosphere and the biosphere, because the air temperature changes
The hydrosphere and the geosphere, because water is moving across land
The geosphere and the biosphere, because the ground is supporting the water
The atmosphere and the geosphere, because the mountain receives sunlight
hints: Melted snow is water, which belongs to one sphere. The mountain and valley are part of another sphere.
Focus on what is actually moving from one place to another.

problemText: A student correctly identifies that a scene contains soil, rain, a plant, and air. The student then claims this proves all four spheres are interacting with each other. Is the student correct, and why?
choices: Yes, because the student was able to identify and name all four of Earth's spheres present in the scene they observed
Yes, because rain is water from the atmosphere moving to the geosphere where it falls on the soil and plant, which demonstrates interaction between multiple spheres
No, because identifying that all four spheres are present is not the same as describing what specific matter or energy moved between two of them
No, because simply seeing all four spheres in one location does not prove they exchanged matter or energy in a way that counts as an interaction
hints: Think about the difference between naming all four spheres and actually describing an interaction.
What three pieces of information do you need to state an interaction?

problemText: A coal-burning power plant releases smoke containing ash and gases high into the sky. A student labels this as an atmosphere-only event because the smoke rises into the air. Explain why this student's reasoning is incomplete, and identify the correct interaction taking place.
choices: The student is correct; the smoke rises into the air and therefore stays entirely within the atmosphere without touching or involving any other sphere
The student forgot that air itself is part of the geosphere, so the event is entirely within one sphere
The student did not realize that burning coal involves living things, so the biosphere is also interacting with the atmosphere during the burning process
The student ignored that the coal and ash come from the geosphere, so the interaction is geosphere-to-atmosphere, not just within the atmosphere
hints: Where does coal come from? What is coal made of?
Remember that naming an interaction requires identifying the two spheres involved AND what specific matter is moving between them.

problemText: Two identical lakes sit side by side. Lake A is surrounded by forest with lots of trees and plants. Lake B is surrounded by bare rock with very little life. During a heavy rainstorm, the water in both lakes rises by the same amount. However, Lake A's water stays much clearer than Lake B's water after the storm. Which spheres are interacting differently between the two lakes, and what explains the difference?
choices: Lake B has geosphere-to-hydrosphere interaction bringing loose rock and soil into the water, while Lake A has less of this interaction because the forest's roots and plants hold soil in place
The atmosphere and hydrosphere interact at both lakes equally during the rainstorm, but Lake A's water stays clearer because the trees filter out particles before they enter the lake
Lake A's forest is part of the biosphere and uses its roots to absorb and remove mud particles that would otherwise make the water cloudy, while Lake B lacks this filtering ability
The geosphere interacts with both lakes in the same way, but Lake A's forest canopy breaks the force of raindrops so less soil washes into the water compared to Lake B
hints: Think about what prevents soil from washing into Lake A but allows it to wash into Lake B.
Roots and plant matter can affect how easily loose material moves from one sphere to another.

problemText: A limestone cave contains stalactites (rock formations hanging from the ceiling). These form when water drips from the cave roof and leaves tiny bits of dissolved mineral behind each time a drop falls. Over thousands of years, these deposits build up into the hanging formations. Identify all the spheres involved in this process, name the specific matter moving, and trace the complete path of that matter through at least two spheres. Which statement best describes this interaction?
choices: The geosphere and atmosphere interact when water vapor in the cave air condenses into liquid drops that eventually build the stalactites over a long period

Water from the hydrosphere carries dissolved minerals from the geosphere and deposits them back into the geosphere, with the atmosphere playing a role by allowing water to evaporate and recondense in the cave
The biosphere creates the water that forms the stalactites by breaking down limestone rock through chemical weathering processes that happen over many years of biological activity
The geosphere and hydrosphere interact to form the stalactites as minerals dissolve and redeposit, but the atmosphere cannot be involved in this process because caves are enclosed spaces underground
hints: Follow the water: where does it come from, what does it carry, and where does it end up?
Think about how water gets inside the cave in the first place, and whether air inside a cave is truly separate from the air outside.

problemText: Which of the following is the correct definition of evaporation?
choices: A change of state that occurs only when water reaches boiling point and undergoes a rapid phase transition to steam
Liquid water changing into invisible water vapor when energy from the sun warms it
The process by which tiny water droplets combine together inside clouds through collision and fusion to eventually form precipitation
The movement of water from Earth's surface upward into the atmosphere in the form of liquid precipitation
hints: Evaporation is a change of state from liquid to gas, not a boiling process.
Look for the choice that mentions energy from the sun and water vapor specifically.

problemText: A wet towel hanging on a clothesline on a warm, sunny day becomes completely dry by evening, even though it never rained and nobody wrung it out. What process caused the water to leave the towel and enter the air?
choices: Condensation, because water vapor in the air cooled down and changed back into liquid droplets that soaked into the towel fibers
Precipitation, because moisture was released from clouds in the sky and fell as rain or mist onto the towel throughout the day
Evaporation, because energy from the sun warmed the liquid water on the towel until it changed into invisible water vapor
Freezing, because the towel was exposed to cold nighttime temperatures that turned the water molecules into solid ice crystals
hints: What happens first when liquid water on a surface is warmed by sunlight?
A wet object drying in the sun involves water leaving the surface as an invisible gas, not joining droplets or falling from the sky.

problemText: A weather balloon carrying instruments rises high into the atmosphere on a summer morning. As it climbs higher and higher, the air around it becomes colder. If water vapor is present in that air, what will happen to the water vapor as the temperature drops?
choices: The water vapor will evaporate even more rapidly as temperatures decrease, which causes the air to hold more moisture and prevents any visible clouds from forming
The water vapor will remain invisible and gaseous because condensation only occurs when air is heated by direct sunlight rather than cooled by altitude
The water vapor will transform into ice crystals that fall as precipitation before the air temperature drops low enough to cause any condensation to occur
The water vapor will condense into tiny liquid droplets because cooling causes the gas to change back into a liquid
hints: Condensation is the reverse of evaporation—it is what happens when a gas cools.
Tiny liquid droplets floating in air are what form a cloud; think about what causes them to appear.

problemText: Over the course of a day, the following sequence of events occurs at the ocean: first, bright sunlight heats the surface of the water all morning; next, by afternoon, a thick, dark cloud forms above the same area of ocean; finally, by evening, heavy rain falls from the cloud onto the ocean surface. Which of the following correctly matches each event to the water-cycle process that caused it?
choices: Sunlight causes evaporation; the cloud forms because of condensation; rain is precipitation
Sunlight causes condensation; the cloud forms because of evaporation; rain is precipitation
Sunlight causes precipitation; the cloud forms because of evaporation; rain is condensation
Sunlight causes evaporation; the cloud forms because of precipitation; rain is condensation
hints: Remember the order: energy warms water first, then vapor rises and cools, then droplets fall.
A cloud is made of tiny droplets, so what process turns invisible vapor into visible droplets?

problemText: A student claims that a puddle disappears on a cool, cloudy afternoon because the water evaporated and then immediately fell back down as very light precipitation that she could not see. Using what you know about the water cycle, explain why this claim does not match what the lesson taught about how evaporation, condensation, and precipitation actually work.
choices: Evaporation requires temperatures above 80 degrees Fahrenheit, so it cannot happen during cool afternoons or cloudy weather
The water vapor would need to cool and condense into droplets first before precipitation could fall, and those visible droplets would form a cloud that she could see
Precipitation can only take the form of large raindrops or snowflakes, never as a fine mist or drizzle, so any water falling would be obvious to an observer
A puddle loses water only through freezing and sublimation on cool days, not through evaporation, so the student's observation does not match the water cycle process
hints: Condensation and precipitation are separate steps—vapor must become liquid droplets in a visible cloud before they can fall.
Think about what a cloud actually is and whether invisible precipitation makes sense given the definition of the water cycle.

problemText: A river running through a desert region receives no rain for an entire summer, yet the river continues to flow and does not dry up completely. Scientists observe that water is evaporating from the river's surface throughout the day. Using your understanding of the water cycle and the lesson's definition of the pathway, construct an explanation for how the river can continue to have water available for evaporation even though no local rain is falling on it.
choices: The river water evaporates continuously but immediately recondenses into liquid form and returns to the river as a localized cycle that does not rely on external water sources
The river has an underground spring beneath it that continuously pumps fresh water into the riverbed to replace any water lost to evaporation during the summer months
Water that evaporated from the river during previous seasons condensed and fell as precipitation in the mountains upstream, where it eventually flowed back to the river as surface runoff
The desert plants surrounding the river absorb water from the ground through their root systems and then release it back into the river through transpiration during daylight hours
hints: The lesson stops at the surface—what happens to water after precipitation reaches the ground is outside this lesson's scope, but you can use that idea to think about where the river's supply comes from.
Evaporation can happen from any exposed water surface, including rivers, and the water cycle repeats—consider where precipitation that fell months ago could have ended up.

problemText: When rain falls on a sloped parking lot, the water cannot soak into the sealed pavement. What term describes the water that flows downhill across the surface of the parking lot?
choices: Transpiration
Infiltration
Runoff
Recharge
hints: Think about water moving across the surface rather than soaking in.
This is the water that parking lots have to direct toward storm drains.

problemText: Two identical patches of ground receive the same gentle rainfall. One patch is made of loose, dug-up soil; the other is hard-packed clay. Which patch will have more water soaking down into the ground, and why?
choices: The clay patch, because packed ground stops water from running off.
The clay patch, because impermeable ground forces all water to stay near the surface.
Both patches will absorb the same amount, because rainfall is identical.
The loose soil patch, because loose ground is permeable and lets water soak in more easily.
hints: Recall what 'permeable' means and how the material itself affects water's path.
Think about what happens when you pour water on sand versus on hard clay.

problemText: A gardener digs a hole and observes that in the upper portion, soil feels damp but has air pockets mixed in with the water. Deeper down, all the spaces between soil particles are completely filled with water. Where is the water table located relative to the gardener's observation?
choices: The water table is somewhere between the upper damp zone and the lower completely wet zone, marking the boundary between them.
The water table is at the surface of the ground, since water is already present in the upper soil layer where the gardener is digging.
The water table is far below the gardener's hole, because water only exists deeper underground and not in the upper portions of soil.
The water table is above the surface of the ground, because underground water pressure forces it to rise higher than the surrounding soil and rock layers.
hints: The water table is a boundary, not just a place where water exists.
Above the table, air and water mix; below it, only water fills the spaces.

problemText: A town's well is drilled to a depth of 35 meters. The local water table is currently at 20 meters below the surface. A prolonged dry period causes the water table to drop by 8 meters. After the water table drops, will the well still reach water, and by how much less margin than before?
choices: No, the well is now too shallow; the water table at 28 meters is deeper than the 35-meter well.
Yes, the well reaches water at a margin of 7 meters below the new water table depth.
Yes, the well reaches water at a margin of 15 meters below the new water table, compared to 15 meters before.
No, because any drop in the water table means all wells in the area run dry.
hints: Calculate the new water table depth (20 − 8), then subtract it from the well's fixed depth.
A well stays wet as long as its depth exceeds the water table depth.

problemText: During a rainstorm, some water falling on a field infiltrates into the soil. Of that infiltrated water, some reaches the saturated zone below the water table and enters an aquifer, but some water stops in the upper soil layer and is absorbed by plant roots. Describe what happens to the water taken up by plant roots and explain how it stays part of the water cycle.
choices: It is locked into the soil particles permanently and never escapes from underground or returns to the water cycle after being absorbed.
The plant absorbs it into its cells and keeps it stored there indefinitely, so the water no longer participates in any part of the water cycle.
The plant releases much of it back into the atmosphere as water vapor through a process called transpiration, continuing the water cycle.
It percolates slowly downward through the soil layers and eventually replenishes the aquifer below the water table through underground recharge.
hints: Consider what 'transpiration' means and when the lesson mentions it.
This path keeps water in the cycle even though it did not reach the saturated zone.

problemText: A region experiences a very heavy, sudden rainstorm. One area receives water on compacted, nearly impermeable soil; a second area has the same soil but with visible cracks running through the underlying rock. Explain why the second area will have less runoff than the first, and trace one pathway that the infiltrated water might take in the second area after it enters the ground.
choices: The cracks in rock have no meaningful effect on how water moves through soil, so both areas will experience identical runoff and the same amount of infiltration.
The cracks in rock collect water at the surface and trap it there, allowing more evaporation to occur while infiltrated water accumulates in the unsaturated zone just below the surface.
The cracks in rock compress the soil material around them, making the second area more compacted and actually causing it to produce more runoff than the first area.
The cracks in rock allow infiltration into the ground, reducing runoff. The infiltrated water soaks downward and may reach the water table, entering the saturated zone of an aquifer.
hints: Cracks make the ground more permeable, creating pathways for water to enter rather than flow across the surface.
Trace what 'infiltrate' means and what happens to water once it enters the ground through cracks.

problemText: A river tumbles rocks along its rocky bed, chipping off small pieces of stone. This process breaks the rock into smaller pieces without changing what the rock is made of. What is this type of weathering called?
choices: Deposition
Chemical weathering
Erosion
Mechanical weathering
hints: The rock is being broken into smaller pieces right where it sits.
Think about whether the rock's material is changing or just its size.

problemText: Rainwater seeps into a crack in a limestone cliff and slowly dissolves part of the rock over many months, making the crack wider and eventually loosening a chunk that falls. Which type of weathering caused the rock to loosen, and why?
choices: Chemical weathering, because rainwater dissolved part of the limestone, changing what it was made of
Mechanical weathering, because the freeze-thaw cycle of water in the crack pushed the rock apart physically without changing its composition
Erosion, because water is carrying the loosened piece away from the cliff face and transporting it to a new location downstream
Chemical weathering, because the rock is located near water for a long time and the water seeping through it causes gradual decomposition
hints: Look at what actually changed about the rock itself, not just its location.
Dissolving is a chemical change—the rock is not the same substance afterward.

problemText: A fast stream carries gravel, sand, and mud downstream for several miles. When the stream enters a wide, slow-moving lake, it suddenly slows down and drops most of its sediment in a fan-shaped pile at the river's mouth. What is the name of this landform, and what caused the river to drop its load?
choices: A floodplain, because the river spreads out over flat land and deposits sediment across a wide area during floods
A delta, because the river lost enough speed to carry the sediment when it met the calm lake water
A canyon, because the river is cutting downward into rock and the flowing water erodes the streambed over time
A delta, because the river's sediment was too heavy to float in fresh water and sinks to the bottom due to gravity
hints: Deposition happens wherever moving water slows down.
Think about what changed about the water's speed and power when it entered the lake.

problemText: Over many years, a river flows past a sandstone ridge, weathering small grains loose from the rock face. The river carries these grains downstream and spreads them across a wide floodplain every time it floods. Explain what must happen at the sandstone ridge first, what happens next as the river carries the grains, and finally what causes the grains to settle out on the floodplain.
choices: Erosion breaks grains loose at the ridge; weathering carries them downstream; deposition drops them on the floodplain when the water slows down
Mechanical weathering carries grains from the ridge; chemical weathering dissolves them downstream; deposition rebuilds them on the floodplain as new rock
Weathering breaks grains loose at the ridge; erosion carries them downstream; deposition drops them on the floodplain when the floodwater spreads out and slows
Weathering and erosion happen at the same time at the ridge; deposition drops grains whenever the river is moving slowly enough to lose carrying power
hints: Remember the order: rock must be loosened before it can be carried, and carried before it can be dropped.
Deposition happens where water loses the speed to carry its load—what happens to floodwater when it spreads out across flat land?

problemText: A fast mountain river tumbles rocks against each other, grinding chips loose from a boulder. Later, during a flood, that same river spreads out over flat land beside it and drops a layer of fine mud. The boulder and the floodplain sediment were both affected by moving water, but in different ways. Which statement correctly describes what happened to each?
choices: Both the boulder and the floodplain sediment were weathered by the river's mechanical action on rock
The boulder was weathered by fast water grinding; the floodplain sediment was weathered by slow water dissolving minerals
The boulder was eroded into chips; the floodplain sediment was also eroded by the spreading floodwater
The boulder was mechanically weathered at its location; the floodplain sediment was deposited where the river slowed down
hints: Weathering, erosion, and deposition are three different jobs, not the same thing.
What was already loose material ready to be moved, and where did it end up?

problemText: Over millions of years, a river has carved the Grand Canyon by repeatedly weathering rock loose from its bed and walls, then carrying that loose sediment miles downstream and depositing it far away in a delta. Meanwhile, a different river nearby flows through a wide valley and floods every year, slowly building up a thick, soft floodplain beside it instead of a canyon. Both rivers do weathering, erosion, and deposition, yet they produce opposite landforms—one cuts down and one builds up. Explain why these opposite outcomes occur, even though both rivers run water over rock year after year.
choices: The canyon river keeps eroding its own bed and walls in the same spot for millions of years, carrying sediment away and leaving a deep cut behind; the floodplain river spreads out and drops its sediment right beside the channel, building up the nearby land rather than cutting it down

The canyon river has a steeper slope and faster current that transports sediment far downstream before depositing it, so the river channel itself remains narrow and deep, while the floodplain river has a gentle slope and slower current that causes sediment to settle nearby, gradually raising the ground surface beside the channel

The canyon river flows through an area with less precipitation and harder rock types that weather slowly over time, while the floodplain river flows through an area with more rainfall and softer rock types that weather quickly and accumulate sediment in a wide flat valley

The canyon river's erosive power is concentrated in a single narrow channel that cuts downward through solid bedrock, while the floodplain river's sediment is spread across a wide area when it floods, and the sediment is fine enough to stay suspended rather than settling and building layers
hints: Think about where the sediment ends up in each case—does it stay nearby or get carried far away?
A canyon forms where erosion carries sediment away; a floodplain forms where that sediment is dropped. What is different about where deposition happens in each setting?
